concept.name: Source provenance
concept.definition: Information about the entities, activities, and agents involved in producing a piece of data or content, which can be used to assess its quality, reliability, or trustworthiness. The W3C PROV family of specifications defines an interoperable model (PROV-DM), ontology (PROV-O), and serializations for representing and exchanging such provenance.
concept.intuition: A chain of custody for information: where did this claim come from, who produced it, and what processing steps touched it along the way.
concept.mechanics: Provenance records describe entities (data artifacts), activities (processes that generated or transformed them), and agents (responsible parties), linked by relations such as wasGeneratedBy, wasDerivedFrom, and wasAttributedTo. Systems attach these records to data items so consumers can audit origins and transformations.
concept.failure_modes: Provenance breaks when any stage of a pipeline fails to record it (gaps in the chain), when records themselves are falsified or detached from the data, or when transformations aggregate many sources so finely that attribution becomes meaningless.
concept.misconceptions: Provenance is not a guarantee of truth — it tells you where data came from, not whether the source was right. Recording a source URL is only the weakest form of provenance; transformations and agents matter too.
concept.example: An entry in this library records that its definition was derived from an SEC rule release, fetched on a specific date, by a specific review process — so a later auditor can re-fetch the same source and check the claim.

citations.source: W3C, 'PROV-Overview: An Overview of the PROV Family of Documents' (W3C Working Group Note, 2013)
